title: Indra's net
hook: a net of jewels in which each jewel reflects every other (Flower Garland, as Huayan explains it)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vimalakirti answered the question of non-duality by saying nothing at all, and later readers heard thunder. Your line: thunderous silence. Did you leave a quiet space for someone? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

Dew hangs on a spider's web at sunrise. Lean in close to one drop and there's the whole garden inside it, tiny and curved. Lean closer and the next drop over is in there too, shining, and inside that drop is this one. Two drops, each holding the other. Now let that run across the whole web. Buddhist teachers in China reached for a picture very like this one to explain a huge sutra of visions. Today's word is that sutra's name: Avatamsaka, the Flower Garland.
screen: `DEW ON A WEB.` → `EACH DROP HOLDS ANOTHER.` → `THE FLOWER GARLAND.`

segments.voice: The Avatamsaka Sutra, in English usually called the Flower Garland, isn't built like an argument. It's built like a vision. Buddhas fill worlds, light pours from them, and the scenes keep opening inside one another. In China a school grew up around it, called Huayan, which is the Chinese name of the sutra. Its teachers had to explain what the sutra was showing, and one of the pictures they used is Indra's net. Here it is, as Huayan tells it. In the heaven of the god Indra hangs a net that stretches out in every direction. At every knot in the net there's a jewel. Each jewel is polished so clear that it reflects every other jewel in the whole net. And each of those reflections holds the reflections of all the others, on and on, without end. Look into one jewel and you're looking at the entire net. The point isn't only that everything is connected. A string of causes would be connected too: the farmer, the rain, the truck, the cup of coffee. Huayan says more than that. Each thing actually holds the whole. One in all, all in one. And here's the detail that's easy to miss: the jewels don't melt into one big glow. Each stays a single, particular jewel, in its own place on the net, and that is exactly why it can reflect the others. Tradition says a Huayan teacher once showed this to a ruler of China by setting mirrors all around a lamp, so the one flame appeared everywhere at once. The net shows up in small places too: one person's mood filling a whole room, a whole family visible in one child's face.
screen: `A SUTRA BUILT LIKE A VISION.` · `A NET OF JEWELS IN INDRA'S HEAVEN.` · `EACH JEWEL SHOWS THE WHOLE NET.` · `EACH JEWEL STAYS ITSELF.` · then, large: `EACH REFLECTS ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: look at reflections in glass. Find something that reflects. A window, a glass of water, a dark phone screen, the back of a spoon. Settle, breathe, and look. See what's caught there: the room, the light, maybe your own face. Then look again, more slowly, and notice that the glass is showing things it isn't, while staying exactly itself. If there's a second reflecting surface nearby, see whether one shows the other. Rest with the looking. The bell holds the time.
Avatamsaka. The Flower Garland Sutra, whose Huayan teachers pictured everything as a net of jewels, each one reflecting all the rest. Today's word.
Your line: each reflects all. Today, when one person's mood changes a room, notice how much of everyone was in it. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In the Huayan tradition of China, and in schools that grew from it in Korea and Japan, Indra's net is a classic teaching image for how all things contain and reflect one another.

original.note: Sanskrit: a garland or ornament. the name of the sutra Huayan teachers built on.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pretty picture of everything being connected.
what it means: a net with a jewel at every knot, each jewel reflecting all the others, so one jewel shows the whole net.
what a scholar hears: the Huayan school used the image to teach that each thing contains all things while staying itself.
